title: A State grant and a City contract for the same kind of work
question: Where does a State grant's stated purpose match what the City paid the same organization for in the same year?
finding: 184 organization-years pair a State grant serving San Francisco with a City contract on the same theme (35 outside the arts); in 22 both sides are $100,000 or more. The largest: YMCA of San Francisco, fiscal 2024, child care places and buildings (State $1,999,999; City $2,156,405); Urban Alchemy, fiscal 2023, shelter and homeless services (State $1,440,000; City $3,070,767); Horizons Unlimited of SF, fiscal 2024, mental health and drug treatment (State $1,000,000; City $1,223,382); Wu Yee Children's Services, fiscal 2024, child care places and buildings (State $1,000,000; City $751,303). Charging one cost to two is not, and a shared theme does not show a shared cost.
how: For each State grant on the California Grants Portal that lists San Francisco as an area served, the project title and description were sorted into ten plain themes by keyword (child care, small-business advice, job training, digital skills, shelter, violence prevention, mental health and drug treatment, meals, legal help, arts). The same organization's City contracts paid in the City fiscal year with the same number were sorted the same way, by contract title and paying department. A row is a State grant and a City contract of $10,000 or more on the same theme; the largest of each is shown. Ranked by the smaller of the two amounts.
limits: This is a keyword match on short titles, so it shows the same kind of work, not the same project, site or cost. The State file records a required matching amount beside some of these grants. City contract titles are terse and some are only a number, so real overlaps are missed and loose ones caught. State and City fiscal years share a label but a State project may start a year later. Only a comparison of the two budgets, or an audit, could show one cost claimed twice.
